extracted.intended_audience: readers of political philosophy; lawmakers; students of law and political theory; general educated public
extracted.subtask_description: A political-philosophical statement of principles delimiting when society (public opinion or the state) may legitimately intervene in individuals' conduct, with illustrative applications (religion, taste, trade, Sabbath laws, temperance, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual non-accountability for self-regarding actions
rubrics_metrics.description: “The individual is not accountable to society for his actions, in so far as these concern the interests of no person but himself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society may express dislike only by advice, instruction, persuasion, and avoidance by other people; it should not punish or coerce persons for conduct that affects only themselves. Examples: personal tastes, opinions, modes of living, private amusements; these are matters of individual concern unless they harm others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability for other-regarding (harmful) actions
rubrics_metrics.description: “For such actions as are prejudicial to the interests of others, the individual is accountable, and may be subjected either to social or to legal punishment, if society is of opinion that the one or the other is requisite for its protection.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conduct actually harms or threatens the interests of others, society may legitimately use social sanctions or legal penalties to protect itself. The central test is whether the conduct prejudices others' interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damage or probability of damage does not always justify interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Although damage or probability of damage to others can alone justify interference, it must not be supposed that therefore it always does justify such interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many legitimate pursuits necessarily cause pain or loss to others (e.g., competition, professional success). Society should not intervene for incidental or unavoidable opposition of interests; intervention is justified mainly when the means used are contrary to general interest (fraud, treachery, force) rather than when outcomes merely disadvantage others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between social acts and individual acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts that are 'social' (affecting the interests of others or society) fall within society's jurisdiction, while purely individual acts (self-regarding) do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: trade is a social act and can be regulated; selling goods affects the public and may justify regulation (e.g., to prevent fraud/adulteration). By contrast, private consumption and personal tastes are individual acts and should be left to the individual unless they produce social harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion is an unreliable basis for legislation on self-regarding conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: On questions of self-regarding conduct, the opinion of an overruling majority is quite as likely to be wrong as right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Majorities often project their own tastes and preferences and may ignore the convenience or pleasure of those they censure. Legislating private conduct on the basis of popular disapproval risks enforcing majority tastes rather than preventing genuine harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society's responsibility is education and influence, not later punishment for weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: Society has had the whole period of childhood and nonage in which to try whether it could make its weaker members capable of rational conduct in life; it cannot wait till they do something irrational and then punish them for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If society allows people to grow up 'mere children' it is to blame for consequent irrational acts; proper recourse is education, upbringing, and non-coercive influence rather than punitive interference with private conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coercive enforcement of prudence or temperance risks backlash
rubrics_metrics.description: Resort to coercion in personal concerns tends to discredit and frustrate the better means of influencing conduct; some persons will rebel and do the opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coercive laws intended to enforce temperance or prudence can provoke defiance among independent characters and harden opposition. Historical example: backlash against Puritan moral intolerance during and after Charles II.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting self-regarding misconduct can be salutary by showing consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Where conduct does no wrong to others but is supposed to do great harm to the agent himself, the example, on the whole, must be more salutary than hurtful, since, if it displays the misconduct, it displays also the painful or degrading consequences attendant on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observing the natural consequences of others' self-regarding misconduct may deter imitation more effectively than prohibition; thus allowance can serve educative and preventive functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the doctrine that the public has a right to enforce moral/perfectibility standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that every individual's claim to others' moral, intellectual, and physical perfection entitles them to demand legislation to correct deviations is monstrous and acknowledges no right to freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'social rights' theory—i.e., that each person has a vested interest that everyone else act exactly as he thinks proper—would justify any violation of liberty. Legislation should not be a tool for enforcing a majority's conception of perfection or moral taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal restrictions must be grounded in direct social interest, not religious motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrictions (e.g., Sabbatarian legislation, prohibiting amusements) can only be defended when they protect others' direct interests; they cannot be justified merely by being 'religiously wrong.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspending industry on a day may be justified where others' work patterns make it necessary, but prohibiting amusements or leisure on religious grounds alone is improper. The state has no commission to avenge supposed offences to the Deity that are not also wrongs to fellow-creatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation where conduct produces social disorder or public burden
rubrics_metrics.description: When private acts (or markets) produce social disorder, insecurity, inequality of burdens, or public expense, they present grounds for regulation because they invade others' social rights (e.g., traffic in strong drink argued to destroy security, invade equality, create social cost).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the social consequences of certain private practices are demonstrably harmful to others (crime, disorder, public cost), regulation may be justified. But the claim must be precise and limited to the social effects, not expanded into a general right to enforce moral preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free trade and minimal market regulation unless necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments were once thought to have to fix prices and regulate manufacture, but it is now recognised that cheapness and good quality are most effectively provided by leaving producers and sellers free, subject to the check of buyers' freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Market restraints are wrong insofar as they fail to produce desired results; public control is justified primarily to prevent harms such as fraud or adulteration, not to micromanage production and prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive harms are tolerable unless produced by wrongful means
rubrics_metrics.description: When an individual pursuing a legitimate object necessarily causes pain or loss to others (overcrowded profession, competitive examination), society admits no right in the disappointed to immunity from such suffering; it interferes only when wrongful means (fraud, treachery, force) are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine competitive disadvantages are a lawful part of social life; the line for intervention is the presence of illegitimate methods rather than the mere fact of others being harmed by success.
